title: Why did people want to tear down the Eiffel Tower?
subject: art
description: In 1887, the biggest names in French arts and letters demanded that work stop on a "factory chimney." Twenty years later, nobody could picture Paris without it.
author: dusan-nikolic

hero.hook: Before it became the symbol of Paris, it was a "hateful column of bolted sheet metal" that people dreamed of pulling down.

blocks.text: On **March 31, 1889**, Gustave Eiffel climbed to the top of his tower and raised the French flag. At **300 meters**, it was the tallest structure ever built by human hands. It had taken a little over two years, about **18,000 iron parts** and **2.5 million** rivets.

Today it is the symbol of France. But in 1887, when work began on the [[Champ de Mars]], part of Parisian high society cried scandal. Writers, painters and architects demanded that the project be abandoned. How did the most hated monument of its day become the most loved?

sections.title: A tower built to last twenty years

blocks.text: In **1889**, France marked the centenary of the Revolution with the [[1889 Universal Exhibition]], a great fair where every nation showed off its progress. To mark the entrance, the government launched a competition in **1886**: "a tower of 300 meters." The plan submitted by the engineering firm of [[Gustave Eiffel]] beat about a hundred rival proposals.

blocks.caption: The building site on the Champ de Mars in 1888: the four piers reach the first floor.

blocks.text: Construction began on **January 28, 1887**. The contract was clear: Eiffel would run the tower for **20 years**, and then it would be dismantled. Nobody was building it for eternity. But some people did not even want to wait for the opening.

Before the tower, Eiffel's firm designed the iron framework of the Statue of Liberty, presented to the United States in 1886. The skeleton that holds the statue upright came out of the same workshops in Levallois-Perret.

On **February 14, 1887**, the newspaper *Le Temps* published the [[Artists' Protest]]. Around fifty signatures: Guy de Maupassant, Charles Gounod, Alexandre Dumas fils, and Charles Garnier, the architect of the Opera. They denounced a "useless and monstrous" tower, a "gigantic black factory chimney" that would crush Notre-Dame and the Louvre.

blocks.caption: Gustave Eiffel, the engineer whose name the tower carries.

blocks.text: Behind the question of taste lay a question of class. The nineteenth-century [[bourgeoisie]] loved the old styles, the columns and pediments inherited from antiquity. A bare iron spire with no ornament had, in their eyes, "no artistic merit." And the tower was unsettling in another way: during the six months of the Exhibition, nearly **2 million** visitors went up, workers and bourgeois mixed together in the same elevators. The protests were brushed aside.
The story goes that Guy de Maupassant often lunched at the tower's restaurant. It was, he said, the only place in Paris from which you could not see it.

The twenty years went by. In **1909**, the government had to decide: dismantle or keep. In the meantime, Eiffel had done everything he could to make his tower indispensable. He set up an office on the third floor, ran weather and astronomical observations there, and lent the summit to physicists for experiments on falling bodies and air resistance.

blocks.caption: The tower's wireless telegraphy station in 1914: the antennas run from the summit down to the Champ de Mars.

blocks.text: The decisive argument was military. From **1903**, [[wireless telegraphy]] antennas were strung from the top. During World War I, the tower's station jammed German communications and intercepted their messages. The "factory chimney" had become a strategic ear. Even the poets changed their minds: for Apollinaire, it was the "shepherdess" of the bridges of Paris, a symbol of a modern and optimistic future.

sections.title: Paris can no longer be imagined without it

blocks.text: Since 1889, about **300 million** people have climbed the tower. Today it welcomes nearly **7 million** visitors a year from all over the world. It no longer serves as a laboratory, but it still carries antennas: television, radio, air-quality monitoring.

events.title: A permanent reprieve
events.detail: The government gives up on dismantling the tower.

blocks.text: The iron giant outlived its contract, its detractors and its lack of "artistic merit." The critics wanted to protect Paris from the tower. A century later, it is the tower that stands for Paris in the eyes of the whole world.
Designed to last twenty years and loathed by the artistic elite of 1887, the Eiffel Tower owes its survival to its scientific and then military usefulness. The symbol came afterward.
